nodes.title: Measure-theoretic foundations
nodes.description: Probability uses measure theory to assign consistent weights to events. Random variables transport that structure into observable quantities.

nodes.title: Probability spaces
nodes.description: A probability space has a sigma-algebra of events and a measure of total mass one. It is the base setting for all probabilistic statements.

nodes.title: Measurable random variables
nodes.description: A random variable is a measurable map into a specified state space. Measurability makes questions about its values into measurable events.

nodes.title: Distributions

nodes.title: Product measures

nodes.title: Independence and conditioning basics

nodes.title: Convergence and limit laws

nodes.title: Modes of convergence

nodes.title: Almost sure
nodes.description: Almost-sure convergence means pointwise convergence on an event of probability one. It describes the limiting behavior of almost every sample path.

nodes.title: In probability

nodes.title: In Lp
nodes.description: Lp convergence makes the expected pth power of the error tend to zero for finite p. It controls moments more strongly than convergence in probability.

nodes.title: In distribution
nodes.description: Convergence in distribution means weak convergence of the probability laws. It can hold even when variables are defined on different sample spaces.

nodes.title: Laws of large numbers
nodes.description: Laws of large numbers explain why empirical averages stabilize. Their mode of convergence and moment assumptions determine the exact conclusion.

nodes.title: Borel–Cantelli
nodes.description: Borel–Cantelli relates summability of event probabilities to repeated occurrence. Its converse form needs additional assumptions such as independence.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Weak law
nodes.description: A weak law gives convergence of averages in probability under specified conditions. It justifies large-sample concentration around a mean.

nodes.title: Strong law
nodes.description: A strong law gives almost-sure convergence of averages under suitable hypotheses. It makes a stronger sample-path statement than a weak law.

nodes.title: Characteristic functions and central limits
nodes.description: Characteristic functions encode probability distributions by complex exponentials. Central limit theorems describe normalized fluctuations around average behavior.

nodes.title: Characteristic functions
nodes.description: Characteristic functions encode probability distributions by complex exponentials. Fourier-analytic properties make them effective tools for weak convergence.

nodes.title: Fourier transforms
nodes.description: The characteristic function is the Fourier transform of a probability measure with a fixed sign convention. Independence turns sums into products of transforms.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Uniqueness
nodes.description: A probability law is uniquely determined by its characteristic function. This allows distributional identities to be proved in transform space.

nodes.title: Continuity theorem
nodes.description: Lévy's continuity theorem connects weak convergence with characteristic-function convergence under the continuity-at-zero condition. It is a main bridge from analytic limits to probability limits.

nodes.title: Central limit theory
nodes.description: Central limit theorems describe normalized fluctuations around average behavior. Their generalizations clarify which dependence and tail conditions are admissible.

nodes.title: Classical CLT
nodes.description: The classical independent identically distributed CLT assumes a finite nonzero variance. Centered normalized sums then converge in distribution to a Gaussian law.

nodes.title: Triangular arrays

nodes.title: Selected refinements

nodes.title: Conditional expectation
nodes.description: Conditional expectation is an integrable quantity adapted to a chosen information sigma-algebra. It preserves averages over all events in that information set.

nodes.title: Radon–Nikodym definition

nodes.title: Tower property

nodes.title: Conditional distributions
nodes.description: Conditional distributions describe laws given observed information when appropriate regular versions exist. Their existence is not automatic on arbitrary measurable spaces.

nodes.title: Martingale basics
nodes.description: Martingales formalize processes whose conditional future mean equals their present value. Filtrations and stopping times make the information structure explicit.

nodes.title: Filtrations
nodes.description: A filtration is an increasing family of sigma-algebras. It records information available as time passes.

nodes.title: Adaptedness
nodes.description: A process is adapted when its value at each time is measurable using current information. Adaptedness prevents dependence on future observations.

nodes.title: Examples and stopping times
nodes.description: Random walks and conditional-expectation processes give standard martingales. Stopping times model decisions determined by the information available when stopping occurs.

nodes.title: Martingale theorems
nodes.description: Martingale inequalities control maxima and oscillations without independence of every increment. Convergence and stopping theorems require careful integrability or boundedness conditions.

nodes.title: Inequalities
nodes.description: Martingale inequalities control maxima and oscillations without independence of every increment. These bounds are the main input for convergence results.

nodes.title: Doob inequalities
nodes.description: Doob inequalities bound martingale or submartingale maxima using terminal values under suitable integrability assumptions. They convert endpoint control into pathwise-probability control.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Maximal estimates
nodes.description: Maximal estimates bound the chance or moment of large process excursions. They help establish uniform control over time.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Upcrossings
nodes.description: Upcrossing inequalities bound how often a submartingale oscillates across a fixed interval. Finite upcrossings support almost-sure convergence arguments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Convergence and stopping
nodes.description: Convergence and stopping theorems require careful integrability or boundedness conditions. Without them, intuitively fair-process arguments can fail.

nodes.title: Martingale convergence
nodes.description: Martingale convergence theorems give almost-sure or norm limits under different hypotheses. Uniform integrability is central when preserving expectations in a limit.

nodes.title: Optional stopping hypotheses
nodes.description: Optional stopping requires conditions on the process and stopping time, such as suitable boundedness or integrability. An arbitrary stopping time does not preserve expectation automatically.

nodes.title: Counterexamples

nodes.title: Markov chains and processes
nodes.description: A discrete-time Markov chain evolves through transition probabilities depending only on the current state. Continuous-time Markov models describe evolution without a fixed time step.

nodes.title: Discrete-time chains
nodes.description: A discrete-time Markov chain evolves through transition probabilities depending only on the current state. Long-run behavior is organized by communication and recurrence.

nodes.title: Transition matrices
nodes.description: A transition matrix records one-step probabilities between countable states. Matrix powers describe multiple steps.

nodes.title: Recurrence
nodes.description: Recurrence means return to a state occurs with probability one from that state. Positive recurrence additionally controls the expected return time.

nodes.title: Invariant measures
nodes.description: An invariant measure is unchanged by the transition operator. When normalizable to a probability, it is a stationary distribution.

nodes.title: Continuous-time processes
nodes.description: Continuous-time Markov models describe evolution without a fixed time step. Generators and semigroups relate infinitesimal rates to finite-time transition laws.

nodes.title: Generators
nodes.description: A generator describes the initial rate of change of the evolution operator. Its domain is an essential part of the definition.

nodes.title: Jump chains
nodes.description: A jump chain records successive states visited by a jump process. Holding times supply the additional timing information.

nodes.title: Semigroups

nodes.title: Poisson and renewal processes

nodes.title: Poisson process
nodes.description: The Poisson process models event arrivals at a constant rate. Its independent stationary increments make it a fundamental continuous-time example.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Construction
nodes.description: A Poisson process can be constructed from independent exponential waiting times. This connects counting probabilities to interarrival-time distributions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Independent increments
nodes.description: Counts on disjoint time intervals are independent in a Poisson process. Their means depend only on interval lengths and the rate.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Thinning and superposition
nodes.description: Independent thinning preserves the Poisson form, and independent superposition adds rates. These operations support decomposition and construction of arrival models.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Renewal theory
nodes.description: Renewal theory generalizes Poisson arrivals by allowing nonexponential waiting times. It studies the accumulation and long-run frequency of renewal events.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Renewal equation
nodes.description: The renewal equation relates a renewal quantity to the waiting-time distribution through convolution. It organizes repeated-event calculations recursively.

nodes.title: Reward processes
nodes.description: A renewal reward process accumulates a reward in each cycle. Under suitable integrability, its long-run rate is expected reward divided by expected cycle length.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Limit behavior
nodes.description: Renewal limit theorems describe asymptotic counts and residual waiting behavior. Arithmetic versus nonarithmetic waiting-time laws can change the formulation.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Brownian motion
nodes.description: Brownian motion combines Gaussian increments with continuous sample paths. Brownian martingale tools connect path properties with stopping and variation.

nodes.title: Construction and path properties
nodes.description: Brownian motion combines Gaussian increments with continuous sample paths. These properties create a canonical model of continuous random fluctuation.

nodes.title: Gaussian increments
nodes.description: Brownian increments over disjoint intervals are independent and Gaussian with variance proportional to elapsed time. This determines the finite-dimensional laws.

nodes.title: Continuity
nodes.description: Brownian motion has continuous versions despite its highly irregular paths. Continuity does not imply ordinary differentiability.

nodes.title: Scaling

nodes.title: Martingale characterization

nodes.title: Quadratic variation
nodes.description: Quadratic variation sums squared increments and converges to elapsed time for Brownian motion in the standard sense. It replaces the vanishing quadratic variation of smooth paths.

nodes.title: Reflection principle
nodes.description: The reflection principle relates a Brownian running maximum to terminal Gaussian probabilities. It uses path symmetry after a suitable hitting time.

nodes.title: Stopping arguments

nodes.title: Stochastic integration and SDEs
nodes.description: The Itô integral integrates adapted stochastic processes against Brownian motion. Itô calculus accounts for the nonzero quadratic variation of stochastic paths.

nodes.title: Itô integral
nodes.description: The Itô integral integrates adapted stochastic processes against Brownian motion. It is constructed by an isometry rather than ordinary pathwise variation.

nodes.title: Simple adapted processes
nodes.description: Simple adapted integrands are piecewise constant with values determined at the left endpoints. Their stochastic integrals are finite sums of Brownian increments.

nodes.title: Isometry
nodes.description: The Itô isometry equates the integral's second moment with the expected time integral of the squared integrand. It gives the norm control needed for extension.

nodes.title: Extension
nodes.description: Completion extends the integral from simple processes to an appropriate predictable square-integrable class. This preserves the isometry and martingale properties.

nodes.title: Itô calculus
nodes.description: Itô calculus accounts for the nonzero quadratic variation of stochastic paths. It provides both transformation formulas and solution methods for SDEs.

nodes.title: Itô formula
nodes.description: Itô's formula adds a second-derivative correction to the ordinary chain rule. The correction comes from quadratic variation.

nodes.title: Existence and uniqueness for SDEs
nodes.description: Standard SDE existence and uniqueness theorems use coefficient conditions such as Lipschitz continuity and controlled growth. Different weak and strong notions of solution require separate statements.

nodes.title: Examples
nodes.description: Geometric Brownian motion and Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes give explicit SDE solutions. They illustrate how drift and diffusion affect path and distribution behavior.

nodes.title: Diffusions and advanced processes
nodes.description: Diffusion generators connect stochastic evolution with deterministic PDEs. Advanced process theory studies long-run averages, rare events, and interacting randomness.

nodes.title: Generators and PDE

nodes.title: Kolmogorov equations

nodes.title: Martingale problem

nodes.title: Boundary behavior

nodes.title: Further topics

nodes.title: Stationarity and ergodicity
nodes.description: Stationarity preserves the law under time shifts, while ergodicity rules out nontrivial invariant events. Together they support identification of long-time and ensemble averages in suitable theorems.

nodes.title: Large deviations
nodes.description: Large deviations quantify exponentially small probabilities of atypical behavior. Rate functions replace variance as the main descriptor on that scale.

nodes.title: Interacting systems or random graphs
